title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education The Latest in Literacy 5-9-26
author: Vaites, Karen
summary: This Teacher Appreciation Week edition of Karen Vaites's literacy digest covers research and commentary across multiple fronts. Key items: a RAND study finding secondary ELA classes assign very few full books (0-3 typically), with teachers of disadvantaged students assigning even fewer; two studies confirming the value of pairing decoding and language instruction for struggling readers; a Yondr-pouch cell phone ban study finding limited academic impact but improved student wellbeing and teacher satisfaction; and Fordham Institute report reverberations about reading comprehension instruction. In practice, items cover continuous blending in kindergarten, vocabulary instruction, Doug Lemov's text-centering work, and the compressed classroom-time crisis caused by AI-assisted homework. The EdTech backlash section pivots from saturation coverage to research on short-form video (Carl Hendrick) and AI-generated instructional video (Becky Allen). Vaites provides editorial framing throughout, not merely a link list.
points: - RAND found secondary ELA teachers typically assign 0-3 full books, with teachers of disadvantaged students assigning even fewer -- a curriculum equity gap embedded in book assignment practices. - Cell phone bans via Yondr pouches showed limited academic achievement impact but clear positive effects on student wellbeing and teacher satisfaction; media coverage largely ignored the wellbeing finding. - The Fordham Institute report is sparking renewed calls for state curriculum mandates, with Natalie Wexler highlighting that teachers' grasp of reading comprehension instruction is even weaker than their use of cueing. - The AI-writing crisis is compressing classroom time: teachers moving both reading and writing in-class to prevent AI completion creates an impossible time squeeze when novels and extended writing require sustained time. - Tim Daly's argument that the chalkboard and McGuffey readers were the original force multipliers in education inverts the EdTech improvement narrative -- the most powerful tools may have existed 200 years ago.
quotes: Much of the internet and media treated the study as conclusive -- even though Yondr pouches are no one's idea of the best way to implement cell phone bans, and the bans were all relatively new. Most gave short shrift to the positive news in the study: improved student well-being and increased teacher satisfaction.

Many teachers have discovered that the only way to ensure students read a whole novel, or any complex text, these days is to do the reading in class -- which obviously takes up a huge amount of time. And now students also need to do all their writing in class? It is hard to see how this will work without limiting both reading and writing to extremely short texts.

To the surprise of no one, the study finds evidence that school curriculum is a factor in the number of books assigned. Teachers serving more historically disadvantaged students assigned fewer full books.
By now, everyone has received the memo: there is an Ed Tech backlash. The coverage is getting a little redundant. So I am dialing back the Ed Tech Backlash Watch, in favor of breaking news.
Ed tech is just big tech in a sweater vest.
